utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Have the accused brought in and take him to the witness bench immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters, to the reporters, to the Office of the Prosecutor, to the Defence counsel, and to the accused. Now we can proceed. Mr. Nobilo, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yesterday, at the end of the day, we left off with a description of the incidents in May 1992 between the individual villages, sometimes the villages where the inhabitants were one ethnic group and others where there were several ethnic groups. In terms of time, the first incident that you are charged with occurs in Duhri in August 1992, and it is Count 14 of the indictment. Tell me, between the 12th of May that we mentioned as an incident and the events in Duhri in August, was the situation calm and was Duhri an exception compared to what happened in Kiseljak in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was not an exception. On the contrary, there were several incidents from this period, particularly from the end of April 1992, throughout May, June, July, and August 1992. What characterised these incidents in particular, particularly in the first stage, was that they were individual incidents, sporadic to begin with. Later on, they grew to become incidents carried out by individual groups or villages and, in time, they grew into international or inter-ethnic incidents. I should like to mention in this regard that the incidents that took place in the neighbouring municipalities, that is to say, outside the Kiseljak municipality, also had an effect and, as I say, influenced the instilling of fear and division and gave birth to new incidents. For the most part, what was characteristic up until August 1992, that is to say, until the conflict broke out in Duhri, was that all the incidents, for the most part, broke out at the level of villages, whether they were uni-ethnic villages or villages with a mixed population, Croatian and Bosniak Muslim. So the conflicts usually occurred at the level of the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the political power and authority in Kiseljak, both military and civilian? What was its relationship towards these conflicts and was government power and authority one of the generators of the incidents up until August 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The political rule of the day, and I have in mind the municipal crisis staff of the Kiseljak municipality firstly, for the most part dealt with the consequences of these incidents. The motives or the causes leading up to the incidents were usually for economic reasons, they broke out for either economic or social reasons. That was what triggered them off. The political powers-that-be were not the generators of those divisions at that time, those conflicts or divisions, but was primarily involved in reacting to the consequences and tried to deal with the situation and what it had created and to calm the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us remind the Court, this crisis staff that decided upon all matters in Kiseljak, it was made up of Croats and Muslims, two ethnic groups took part in it. Before we come to the conflict in Duhri ... The answer was ...

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like, for the purposes of the record, to have the answer recorded. In answer to my question, the witness said "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So before we go on to describing the incident that is mentioned in the indictment first, and that is the conflict around Duhri, tell us very briefly, telegraphically, so to speak, in one sentence, could you enumerate the important incidents which upset the international relationships on the eve of the Duhri incident, that is to say, what happened at the end of May and in June and July?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, already on the 13th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, we are listening to you very carefully, of course. I think that you dealt with this yesterday, or didn't you? I noted your question had to do with the previous period, that is, the appointment of the accused to the head of Central Bosnia for May, June, and July, and the accused spoke about incidents in armed Croat villages or non-armed Croat villages. Is that the question that you're asking? I don't want us to go back constantly to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Mr. President. I asked the question, but the witness did not enumerate all the incidents, and the last date yesterday that we encompassed was the middle of May 1992. So now we should like him to enumerate the incidents that took place in the next two months, but very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You had moved to the incident of August 1992. You had begun your examination-in-chief by Count number 14 in the indictment. I just want to be sure what we're doing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I did that so that the Trial Chamber could come to understand why we're talking about the incidents. Our goal is Duhri, but Duhri did not come out of the blue, something preceded Duhri, whereas this was pulled out of a hat, Duhri was sort of pulled out of a hat, but we want to show the genesis of the Duhri incident, what led up to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, very briefly, let us enumerate the conflicts that took place.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 13th of May, 1992, the conflict broke out between the village of Drazevici, that is a Serbian village, and the village of Grahovci, which is a Muslim Bosniak village, both in the Kiseljak municipality, and the consequences of that conflict were that the village of Drazevici was disarmed. On the 14th of May, 1992, another conflict broke out, this time in the village of Brestovsko between the Croats. The participants in the conflict were the Croats. Also, on the 14th of May, 1992, a conflict broke out between the Croatian villages of Donja Podastinje and the Croatian village of Donji Palez. The cause of that conflict was who was to control the roadblock. On the 14th of May, 1992, there was an incident that broke out in the village of Hercezi, where the members of the Territorial Defence forces from the village of Hercezi opened fire on a Croat civilian, the driver of a motor vehicle. On the 14th of May, 1992, in the town of Kiseljak, there was confrontation between the members of the HVO on the one side and the members of the Territorial Defence who allegedly had intended to deblock the city of Sarajevo on that day. Towards the town of Kiseljak, columns of motor vehicles started out from the directions of Visoko, Kresevo, Fojnica, Bilalovac. On the 15th of May, 1992, a Croatian civilian was wounded in the village of Medvjednica by the Territorial Defence forces, and there was considerable difficulty in transporting him to a hospital. On the 16th of May, 1992, in the local community of Gromiljak, conflicts broke out between the Croats on the one side. We had the Croats from the villages of Visnjica, Dolce, and Hercezi, and on the other side the remaining Croats in the villages of the Gromiljak local community. On the 19th of May, we once again had an incident in Duhri and Gornji Palez. Gornji Palez was a Croatian village, Duhri was a Bosniak Muslim village. Trenches were dug. Both sides turned their weapons towards each other; they faced each other. On the 23rd of May, 1992, an incident broke out in the village of Tulica between the Croats and Bosniak Muslims. The Croats were from the village of Azapovici. On that same day, on the 23rd of May, there was another incident in Brestovsko between the Croats, the military recruits, and Croats belonging to the reserve formation of the civilian police. On the 25th of May, the Territorial Defence of Gomionica, a Muslim Bosniak village, dug fortifications, trenches, bunkers, and communicating trenches directed to face the Croatian villages of Krizici and Gornji Podastinje. On the 26th of May, it was rumoured in Kiseljak that the municipal crisis staff was carrying out distribution of military flats, flats belonging to military men, and this had, as its repercussion, the occupation of the entire barracks and the storming of the barracks by practically all the members from the urban area of Kiseljak, both the Croats and the Muslims, predominantly members of the Patriotic League with weapons. People who had weapons carried them on the occasion. On the 27th of May, 1992, in the local community of Gromiljak, there was, after the incident, a division, a rift between the Croatian villages, and they became divided. They were divided into Gromiljak 1 and Gromiljak 2. On the 31st of May, 1992, the municipal crisis staff of Kresevo was confronted with the municipal crisis staff of Kiseljak over questions of competency and authority over the relay station, radio relay station of Cubren and checkpoints were set up or, rather, barricades, at the delineation line between the two municipalities. On the 31st of May, 1992, there was an open armed conflict between Croatian villages, the Croatian villages of Donji Podastinje and the Croatian village of Donji Palez, between the two. The fighting lasted almost until midnight, and after that, the conflict was settled. On the 4th of June, 1992 in Kiseljak, units from outside stormed Kiseljak under the command of Mr. Porobic, Mustafa Porobic, and they told us they were members of the Rijeska Brigada, and they took control of the entire Dalmacija Hotel located in Kiseljak. They threw out about 300 displaced persons, Muslim Bosniaks, from Rakovica who had been put up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you please explain to the Trial Chamber what the Rijeska Brigada was? What was the composition of that unit? Where was the unit set up and equipped, which state, before it arrived in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That afternoon, I talked to the deputy commander of this unit, and he told me that they were members of the Derventa Brigade from Bosanska Posavina, the area called Bosanska Posavina, which, after the Serbs had occupied Bosanska Posavina, had rallied together in the town of Rijeka in the Republic of Croatia. They underwent training in Rijeka and were equipped there with weapons and full military gear, and, having been equipped in that way, they came to Kiseljak and, on that day, were deployed in the Dalmacija Hotel. The composition of the brigade was that the majority of members were Bosniak Muslims, although there were some Croats within the composition of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We can move on, I think, and discuss the following incident.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 5th of June, 1992, four officers were killed belonging to the joint command of the regional staff for Central Bosnia. The killing occurred on the territory of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf in the area which was controlled by the HVO forces and the TO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of those killed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mostly they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Also on the 5th of June, the village of Tulica, a Bosniak Muslim village, opened fire on Croat members in the village of Azapovici, and the unit of Territorial Defence, which was called the detachment, I don't remember the number, the detachment had a number, and it was from Kiseljak, when they launched the operation to deblock Sarajevo, so they opened fire on the backs of the defenders of the HVO who, at that time, were located on a position called Zelena Meraja. On the 11th of June, 1992, the Territorial Defence forces in the area of the Kiseljak municipality stormed Croatian houses, ransacked them, took away weapons from the Croats where they found weapons. On the 14th of June, 1992, the members of the Territorial Defence forces from the village of Bukovica in the Kiseljak municipality also ransacked all the non-Muslim homes. There were several houses belonging to the Serbs, but most of them were owned by Croats, and they seized weapons and military equipment from those houses during the search. On the 15th of June, 1992, the members of the Territorial Defence forces, who represented themselves as being members of TG-1, threatened the Croats in the village of Medvjednica and said that, with the operation to deblock Sarajevo, they would be used as a human shield in breaking through the front lines of the army of the Republika Srpska. On the 15th of June, the Territorial Defence of Bukovica forbade Bakir Alispahic to enter the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Bakir Alispahic was the Muslim commander, together with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. On the 15th of June, 1992, the Territorial Defence of Gomionica set up a counter-infantry minefield in front of its positions facing the Croatian village of Krizici. On the 17th of June, 1992, the commander of the headquarters of the Territorial Defence of Kiseljak disarmed the village of Tulica, the Bosniak Muslim village, and took the weapons to Bukovica. This is a village which is along the front line towards the army of the Republika Srpska. On the 18th of June, 1992, a conflict broke out in Novi Travnik, and what happened was that they tried to gain control of the petrol pump there. The conflict broke out between the HVO and the TO of Novi Travnik. In the night between the 20th and the 21st of June, 1992 in Gornji Vakuf, the commander of the regional staff for Central Bosnia was kidnapped. His name was Zulu. On the 22nd and 23rd of June, 1992, there were conflicts going on in Gornji Vakuf between the members of the HVO and the members of the TO. On the 25th of June, 1992, members of the Hajdarevic family in the local community of Brnjaci opened fire on Croatian houses belonging to the Bosnjak family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Hajdarevics were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were Muslims, and the Bosnjaks were Croats, and this lasted during the night of the 25th of June. On the 18th of June, 1992, members of the Territorial Defence from Visoko arrived in the territory of the Kiseljak municipality and conducted a search of Croatian villages in the border areas of the municipality of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, let me stop you here for a moment because I want to move on to when you were appointed the commander of the Operative Zone, which happened on the 27th of June, but before we move on to that, can you tell me, how did the civilian authorities respond in Kiseljak or Vitez or elsewhere and how you personally responded to these incidents?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was very difficult to respond because both the communications and the command structure had not been established. When I say "difficult," I refer to the commanders of both the Territorial Defence and the HVO and other armed groups. The only way was to go to the site of an incident and to try to persuade those who were in conflict to stop. The civilian authority, in almost all the cases which I have mentioned here, would hold meetings and was attempting to find people who had authority, the local prominent representatives of the Croatian or the Bosniak Muslim communities, and then, in contact and communication with them, would lower tensions and try to overcome the consequences of such conflicts. Myself and Bakir, who worked closely with me at the time, were strangers in this area, and the individuals whom we met were also unknown to us. So it was quite difficult to try to resolve these conflicts and respond to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would it be possible for the civilian authority to conduct any kind of repressive measures, in other words, to arrest some of the people involved and organise their trials, for instance?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, this was not possible, all the more so because some of the armed groups were better armed than the police itself. What further complicated the situation, the judicial system did not function, that is, at the municipality level, and such cases simply could not be prosecuted. The role of the police was, often times, reduced to just registering the incident and responding after the incident, but the full follow-up process was not possible in the area of Kiseljak at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: With this organisation of local power, which was not based on particular laws but rather the conditions, in other words, this mixture of military and civilian power which called itself the crisis staff, what did they consider at that time? Was this lowering of the tensions the task of Bakir Alispahic and yourself or was it their own, that is, the competence of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Bakir Alispahic and I, first of all, were not members of these civilian structures, and we were only asked to report on the preparations for defence in the territory of the municipality, in other words, to report on our work on the front line against the army of the Republika Srpska. We were not considered responsible for the security matters behind the front lines, so the municipal government did not consider us responsible for that, and the chief of the police station in Kiseljak reported on these security matters or it would be the commander of the police station, both of them members of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you and Bakir, despite that, volunteer to go to these villages, talk to people, try to lower the tensions?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I personally went with Bakir on occasion, like to Bukovica and Tulica on the 17th of June when there was this disarming. I talked to everybody in Tulica, to the Bosniak Muslims, and I attempted to at least alleviate the situation because they were left without weapons and they were on the front line. I was also in the village of Grahovci, Han Ploca, sometimes with Bakir, sometimes he would go there by himself, depending on the situation, the need, and our own assessment of the situation; however, I never received an order from any superior, that is, from the municipal crisis staff, to go to some of these villages because they too were aware that both of us were strangers in the area. I believe that Bakir was not even born in the Kiseljak area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You arrived in April and now we're dealing with June. This is what you had promised your wife you would do, that after those two months, you would go back. So what happens now? You not only stayed but now you assumed a new, more responsible role. What was the reason for this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct. I was aware that what I had set out to do, what I thought it was possible to do at the level of the Kiseljak municipality, I had not completed, and I did not conduct all preparations for defence, that is, for preparation and organisation of personnel, as well as the territory. Also I was aware, that is, those two months allowed me to get to know, to get a better picture of the situation in Central Bosnia in general, and, in fact, I saw that as far as the professional military personnel is concerned, especially among the Croats, there were very few of these people, maybe five or six people, who had been active in the former JNA. True, I was able to establish a corps at the level of the Kiseljak municipality, but still there was no structure in place. This was still just the armed population who were facing at least the same, if not even more, danger from the Serbian advances. So my conscience did not allow me to leave this area because I believed this would be like leaving a sinking ship at the time. So this is why I decided to stay on and continue my work without asking for any compensation or any benefits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 27th of June, 1992, you were at a meeting in Grude. This was the first time that you met Boban and the other leaders of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Can you clarify for the Trial Chamber that event and how you became the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I attended the meeting of 27 June, 1992, in Grude, in the basement of Hotel Grude, with the late Mate Boban and other people attending were the commander of the main headquarters of the HVO, whom I met that day for the first time, and also attending was General Roso, and briefly I stated my views to Mr. Boban, my views on the military situation. When I say "briefly," it was a 20- to 30-minute briefing, and after that I, for the most part, talked to the chief of staff of the main headquarters. I discussed Central Bosnia, I discussed different fronts, mostly military matters. After finishing this conversation, I received an order on my appointment as commander of the regional headquarters for Central Bosnia. This order was signed by Mr. Mate Boban and General Ante Roso.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So this was the first time when you met the military and political leadership of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what did you know at that time? What information did you have on the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? What was it? What were the goals? Because you said that in Kiseljak, you basically had an autonomous Croatian-Muslim authority, regardless of any superior authority. So can you tell me, what did you learn about the structure and goals of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and what opinion did you form? What organisation were you becoming a part of?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My first meeting was actually my first direct source of information on what Herceg-Bosna was, that is, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I should say, and my understanding of it was that it was a form of self-organising of the Croatian people for defence against the Serbian aggression. What I remember well and what Mate Boban requested in the conversation with me was that he expected that the members of the HVO, that the army were apolitical and professional and that any kind of politics would be eliminated from the operations of the military. He pretty much literally said: Leave out politics and the political questions, and leave it to the elected representatives of the Croatian people to deal with those. What your duties are are to organise and carry out defence against the Serbian aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was this position acceptable to you? Did you have any political ambitions? Were you a member of the HDZ in Bosnia or outside Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of any political party except that during my training in the military academy, which was at a time of the former Yugoslavia, like any cadet, I was a member of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. When this party fell apart or dissolved, I never joined any other political party, and this was the only position that I felt comfortable with. This is what I repeated a number of times in many meetings with my associates, even later on when I was commander of the regional headquarters, saying that the military personnel within the HVO need to be depoliticised and that they should let the civilian representatives, the elected civilian representatives of the Croatian people, deal with political matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you received an order that you became the military leader of Central Bosnia. Did you also receive a rank at that time? If you did, describe it, please.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive a rank, and under strange circumstances, I should say, for me. When my briefing was completed, General Roso said, and I quote him: "Very well. You will be a major and commander of the regional headquarters for Central Bosnia." And then he looked at a map where the zone of responsibility in Central Bosnia was drawn, and he said, and I quote him, "Well, in fact, this is quite a bit of a territory. In fact, you will be a colonel." After that, I received an order appointing me to the duty of commander of the regional headquarters for Central Bosnia, but I never received a formal decision for the rank of colonel; that is to say, in the former army and in the armies that exist today in this territory, I think that it is by a decree that the ranks are conferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. So you were conferred the rank of colonel even though there were no ranks in the HVO at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. At that time, there was no conferral of ranks in the HVO. There was no basis for establishing a chain of command, so everybody was just a commander and everybody addressed each other as such, starting from just a combat group of three soldiers up to the level of the commander of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Before we move on, let's just clarify something. You became commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia which, at that time, was a very large territory, even larger than the one that you will end up being a commander of later on. Could you say, in a normal army, what rank did you take on at that time and what rank had been the highest rank which you had had in the previous army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Looking from the size of the territory, this would be a rank of the commander of a corps, but this is only if the criterion would be the number of -- if we just look at what rank would be with reference to the number of recruits, that would be the commander of a division. But when I finished my training in 1983, I qualified as a commander of a platoon, and the highest duty I ever had was commander of a company, and for a brief period of time, deputy commander of a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just to clarify it even more for those of us who are not military experts: How many soldiers are in a division, how many in a company?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The standards are pretty much the same in all armies. For a division, it is somewhere between 8.000 and 12.000 soldiers, depending upon what type of division this is, but this is how we were taught in the military academy; and a company is comprised of about 100 to 150 soldiers at the most, again depending upon whether it is an infantry, a mountain, or what type of company it is, so not below 100, not over 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How would you define your military experience up until this assignment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: While you're on that aspect, would you see any value in getting the witness to say what is the size of a corps and what is the rank, the normal rank, of the military officer commanding a corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please, General. In the indictment, "corps" is mentioned several times, like the 3rd Corps. So what would be the rank of an officer commanding a corps and how many soldiers would a corps have?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, a corps is a combined unit, so the number of soldiers also depends, but it varies -- it goes from 25.000 up to 30.000, even 50.000, and even beyond. The way we were taught in the military academy, a corps could be composed of brigades, in other words, let's say, to be composed of ten, or up to ten brigades, and it could be a group of divisions, so that it would have three, perhaps four divisions. In any event, it would have no less than 20.000 soldiers. It is difficult to sort of define it upwards because it depends upon the type of corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What would be the typical rank of the commander of a corps, let's say in just a regular, normal military organisation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the former -- if I speak of the former JNA, and I think that this is the case today as well, it would be Major-General or General who had a certain amount of experience, but he would have to have over 20 years of professional experience in a military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Were you talking about a corps or a division?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is approximately the same. It would have to be at least 20 years of troop experience and it would also have been typical for this commander to have had experience of at least three or four years in some kind of command structure and to have had proper education. Some places it's called wartime, war academy, and some places it's called the national security academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So this is a rank that is several grades above the military academy?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this would be several grades above the simple military academy. I'm talking about the regular procedures. In order to become a commander of a company, you not only had to have completed the military academy but also a special course and to have had at least three years of experience as commander of a platoon. Also, the standard was that a commander of the battalion, in order to become a commander of a battalion, one had to undergo a course, a six-month course leading to that duty or to have an equivalent experience in some type of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How about commander of a corps or a division, what other training was requisite?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A necessary requirement would have been a staff academy which lasted for two years and then one would have had to have experience of a commander of a brigade or a regiment, plus one had to have applied for an exam for General. Also, another requirement was an All People's Defence course or a national security course, so that would be the highest training that was offered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. How would you sum up your experience in the JNA? Were you just a regular troop officer or were you more involved in the training?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Between 1983 and 1986, I was, for the most part, away from troops. I worked with cadets. I worked with the cadets of the academy of reserve --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Excuse me. There was -- the years were '83 to '86, not '93 to '96. [Real-time had "1993" and "1996"]

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. After I graduated from the military academy in 1983 until 1986, I was, for the most part, involved in training, teaching. At that time and later on, I did not take any courses for commanding duties, either for a company or a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let's go back to 1992. In Grude, you were appointed as the chief military person for Central Bosnia. What followed? When did you take over the duty? Who did you meet there? What did you take over in terms of documents, in terms of the organisation of the headquarters for Central Bosnia and so on?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I took over my duties as commander at a meeting held on the 30th of June, 1992, in Gornji Vakuf; it was a meeting which had been convened previously, scheduled previously by the former commander of the regional headquarters for Central Bosnia, Mr. Zulu. At that particular meeting, I availed myself of the few minutes that I had beforehand to inform him of the fact that I had received a command and that I was, in fact, going to take over his command, take over his duties. He told me that he had also been informed of this decision and decree, and that when the meeting was over, he would formally hand over his duties to me. At the end of the meeting in his office, he gave me military documents and a notebook which was called a war journal or war log, and that was my first encounter with a document of that kind, and that was all the documents that he had to give me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the staff in the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The staff comprised of the deputy commander, his deputy, Mr. Luka Sekerija, who was the commander of the municipal headquarters of the HVO for Gornji Vakuf, and he performed the duty of his deputy, he acted as his deputy, because the office of the commander for the regional headquarters were located in the building of the municipal headquarters of the HVO for Gornji Vakuf. However, the deputy did not have any order on appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I would like to ask you for a clarification. General Ante Roso, what was his position before yours?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I don't know what function he had at the time, what rank. I saw him for the first time. On that occasion, he was there together with General Petkovic and they sat round the same table. General Petkovic introduced himself to me for the first time on the occasion and said that he was the chief of the main staff of the HVO and I reported to General Petkovic. I don't know nor did I later see what function he performed within the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So you would report to General Petkovic; is that correct? Did I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: General Petkovic was the chief of the main staff of the HVO at that time. I did not get any information nor did I know the function of General Roso.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Excuse me. Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, you would have understood that General Roso was then speaking with the authority of General Petkovic; is my impression correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In addition to Luka Sekerija, who else was a member of the regional headquarters, regional staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In addition to Luka Sekerija, we had the assistant for information, Mr. Marko Prskalo, and in the main staff, there were two secretaries; however, none of them had any document or order or decree on appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you find any documents relating to fighting and combat operations, and were you able to understand whether this main staff gave out combat orders for Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not come across one single combat document. I asked the commander to give me some documents of that kind, but he said that he had no other documents, and he did not even have a list of commanders of the municipal headquarters listing their names and surnames, and I realised, I understood, that from that office, no commands were issued from that office from any of the commanders, nor was there any communication, in the military sense of the word, with the immediate commanders, subordinate commanders, because the command there, apart from Mr. Zulu, did not have any other people who were appointed, any other individuals appointed to a position in that command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court who the commanders were of the regional headquarters of Central Bosnia before you, and what do you think, why did Boban and Petkovic choose you? What choice did they have? What did your potential professional competition and traits represent in their selection of you in particular?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, I was the fifth commander within a space of one month, barely one month. Before me, I had got to know the commanders of the regional headquarters. One of them was Mr. Pasko Ljubicic. I also knew that for a period of time this duty was performed by Mr. Filip Filipovic. I also was introduced to Mr. Brigadier Zarko Tole, and I also met Mr. Zulu. We would address him as commander. He did not have a rank, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So these then were professional officers in Central Bosnia. Why do you think you were chosen? What criteria led to your election?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. The one who came before you was Mr. Zulu, was it not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So chronologically then, the first was Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, as far as I know, I did not have an insight into their documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you don't know, you can imagine how difficult it is for us. These were your direct predecessors. There were five in one month. There were five in one month. You were the fifth. Before you was Mr. Zulu.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Before Zulu, it was Mr. Zarko Tole. Before him, I think it was Filipovic and Mr. Ljubicic before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, let me just clarify what I mean when I say "I don't know." I know who represented himself as commander to me and introduced himself as commander to me, but I did not see any decree or order as to that appointment. So I was not able to control their documents relating to their appointments. I know that they introduced themselves as such, as being commanders, without actually seeing the appointment decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we take a break now perhaps, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're going to take a break because we're going to have to stop at 12.45, so we're going to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing now. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, let us continue. The last question before the break was what was the possible choice, that is to say, the potential competition you had from the professional officers in Central Bosnia, the competition you had with them, and why do you think you were selected to be the commander for Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in Central Bosnia, I already said that there were very few active military personnel, and the choice was also made on the basis of professionalism and my professional training and education. Besides myself, there was the possibility of choosing as commander and appointing as commander Mr. Ivica Rajic, who had completed the military academy in Rajlovac for air reconnaissance, the air reconnaissance course. This was, for the most part, work with radar stations and the technicality involved in this. That was his particular expertise. Then there was Mr. Mato Lucic, who had completed the higher military academy which lasted for two years, he graduated after this two-year course, and he had been working for a little under one year as commander of a platoon for anti-aircraft defence. There was another candidate, possible candidate, his name was Ivica Zeko, but he was a specialist and trained expert in matters of reconnoitring units, reconnaissance units. At that time in the HVO in the area of Central Bosnia, they were mostly infantry men, that is to say, armed villagers and locals with different types of small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Filip Filipovic was an officer. What were his credentials, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he had graduated from the artillery, and he was, for a time, commander of the regional staff, but very soon he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about your particular field of expertise?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I graduated from the ground forces and infantry at the academy, so for infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we, therefore, conclude that you had the rank of an infantry man, and that is what the HVO had, it had an infantry?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. As an active military man from the JNA, in that particular area, I was the only one holding that particular rank, and my field of expertise was for the infantry. The others worked in Territorial Defence and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you describe to us now the situation that you encountered when you came to the Operative Zone, in the sense of the battleground and front line towards the Republika Srpska, what units existed, what their composition was, so on and so forth? So can we describe the situation in the Operative Zone when you took over as commander?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would need a map to describe the front line.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D539.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May we zoom in with the camera onto the map, please?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: So the first front line under my area of responsibility was the Kupres battleground, and authority over the municipal headquarters of Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I can't see this, and I doubt my colleagues can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. The Judges don't see it very clearly either. I know that it's difficult. As regards you, Mr. Kehoe, there wouldn't be any problem, you can approach the model, and if the witness wants to rise, of course, he can. There's no problem with that. There's the problem with the Judges which is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the camera can't zoom in, Your Honour, then we will put it on the ELMO and then it will be visible to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Whatever is easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps that would be the best thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as we're getting ready to put this on the ELMO, it might be easier for us and the Court if we could get a copy of it so we can take a look at it. It would be easier to examine. If counsel has a copy, it would be easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We would like a copy too. We don't have any copies. So if the court staff can help us in that regard, we would be grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. I will decide that the Tribunal will make available as quickly as possible the map, both for Defence counsel and for Prosecution counsel and, of course, for the Judges. Mr. Registrar, be sure that that is done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. In the meantime, we will do what we can with the ELMO, but that is already a lot of progress. I'm beginning to see things now. General Blaskic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the front in the regional headquarters of Central Bosnia comprised of the following: The Kupres front which included the municipal commands of Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, and then we have part of the front to north-west Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic, are you defining the combat zones or the municipal staffs? I didn't pay careful enough attention. Are the combat zones against the Serbs there or the organisation? Is it the organisation or the combat zones? What is it that you are defining?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, on this map, I wish to show the front and the front lines towards the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps we could limit ourselves to the front lines and forget which commands held which sections. Let's see Central Bosnia under your command, what were the front lines towards the Serbs that they held?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: So the front lines were as follows --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- the Kupres front and the front in north-west Herzegovina, the front Glamocko around the town of Jajce --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the map, we can see that the front line has been moved slightly. Can you tell us when Jajce fell?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Probably the map is outside the time span of the 28th of October. It probably dates back to the end of October, beginning of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the map, it states that the map dates back to December 1992 when Jajce had already fallen.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Jajce fell at the end of October 1992, but when I took over the command, we had a front line up here towards the army of the Republika Srpska. Then there was the Komar pass, Radalj, Lasic, and towards the north towards Teslic. Then we come to the area south of Doboj and onwards, the west slopes of Mount Ozren, Olovo, east of Vares, Mount Zvijezda, Kiseljak, Hadzici, the slopes of Mount Bjelasnica, and the western slopes of Mount Visocica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Part of the front of the municipalities in Sarajevo, that is, the centre of the city, in concrete terms, it was the electricity building up to Vrbanja Most, the bridge, and the Stup municipality and part of the front at Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Those were all the suburbs of Sarajevo, suburban municipalities?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sarajevo was under encirclement, and those, for the most part, were parts of the front. There were seven fronts in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We're going to leave the map for a moment, and we shall be getting a copy to hand round of the map. Can you tell us what situation you encountered? What units of the HVO did you have in Central Bosnia when you took over your command, and how were they organised?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The situation was as follows: It was similar to the situation in the Kiseljak municipality. There were no organised military formations, and in actual fact, each municipality was, in a way, organised, that is to say, there was only a brigade being formed in Usora, it was called the 110th Brigade, but it was still under formation. It still had not been completely established, nor did it have all the formation documents and organisational documents that were required; however, recruits from that area referred to themselves as the Usora Brigade actually prior to the actual establishment of the brigade itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How was the defence organised along the fronts that you mentioned? What model did you pursue?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The defence was organised in such a way that the shifts of armed locals, villagers, would take up certain positions, they would be deployed according to shifts, and the shift would last between one to five days at most. The most numerous armed groups could be referred to as shifts. They were referred to as shifts, and that's what they called themselves. They called themselves shifts and these shifts were mobilised by the offices in the different municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, what happened five days later when one shift completes its term of duty on the front line?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After five days, or after one day sometimes, usually it was a one-day shift, the shift would return to base, that is to say, to the village and the homes, their own homes in the villages, and they would take their weapons with them and ammunition with them and all the military gear that they had been issued. They would then carry on with their daily work. If they were people who were employed in companies, they would go to perform their daily jobs, they would go to work. The peasants would tend to their land, depending upon the season, if it was a season for field work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So that was the situation you encountered. How then did you undertake your duties? What were your methods of work? What were the concrete things that you did as commander of the regional headquarters?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the very beginning, I endeavoured to organise meetings with the commanders of the municipal staff and have them brief me on the existing military situation, although I was fully conscious of the fact that I would not be able to engage in operative command, but I wished to take all the necessary steps to try and influence this or give assistance to the individual commanders. What influenced my activity most were the front lines and the seven fronts that I enumerated. Of course, there were other activities involved. We had to contend with the attackers, and the attacks were not in equal measure on all the fronts. Then there was the time that I had at my disposal, the configuration of the land and logistics. I had to take all this into account. I usually applied two forms of work: One was my individual work, that was one way in which I functioned; and, secondly, we would have joint work together, that is to say, I would hold joint meetings with the commanders of individual municipal headquarters or with the commanders of one of the municipal commands. I would visit them, for example. I would personally visit the front lines, tour the front lines, and have talks there with the soldiers up at the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me, where did you work as the commander of the regional headquarters? Where did you create your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I first took over the duty in Gornji Vakuf, and I stayed there, in other words, I had an office there at the headquarters of the municipal staff of the Gornji Vakuf HVO, and then I sent a proposal, which was agreed to, that I transfer this headquarters to Vitez, to the local commune of Kruscica. There was a motel there, it was called Lovac or "Hunter," and this is where I wanted to set up the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Apart from the headquarters, did you also have a sort of satellite headquarters during 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I had command posts on several fronts. The first command post was in the territory of Kiseljak municipality in the village of Bukve, and later it was transferred to Cubren. Then I had another command post in Jajce, in the village of Blazevici. Additionally, I had a command post in Zepce and a command post in Travnik during the period when the defence of Travnik was at issue. When I say "command post," I, first of all, had in mind certain facilities which would be part of the front line, sometimes there would be shelters or dugouts, and I would normally be there and, along with me, one or two of my associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This was exclusively the front lines?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, the Travnik command post was directly at the front line against the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The main headquarters, apart from these command posts at various front lines, your central command post was in Kruscica. Can you tell me, who lives in Kruscica? Which ethnic group has a majority population there and was there a problem for you there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew, based on information given to me by the municipal headquarters in Vitez, that Kruscica was predominantly inhabited by Bosniak Muslims. However, for me, that was not a problem at all nor did I consider it a problem. The biggest problem I had was that I only had a piece of paper saying that I had this authority; that was the only thing that I actually had. I was not a member of any municipal headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Trial Chamber what were your initial activities; in other words, what did you start with and how did you go about your duties in this new post?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were a number of priorities, and let me try to list them. What I thought that my basic role was, if I was not able to have an operational command of the defence, I felt obliged to exercise certain influence over the combat activities, and what I mean by that is to provide assistance at the most threatened fronts which had been attacked by the aggressor. Then I tried to work together with the commanders of these municipal staffs, that is, Jajce and Bugojno, who were at the front line, to slow down, if this was possible, and, if possible, stop the insurgence and advances of the Serbian forces, and specifically in Jajce, we very soon came to the realisation that we needed to set up a defence, and so I became involved on these fronts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you describe, define, what "missing defence" means in purely military terms?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That means that we were not able to lose -- you were not in a position to lose any more military facilities because in the area of Mrkonjic Grad, we had been squeezed practically into the city centre itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Does that mean that there will be no retreat?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in a way that is what it means, but I also tried to convince commanders at the front lines that what was needed was to increase caution because any further losses would mean the fall of the town of Jajce. Apart from that, I also thought that I needed to work on preparing the ground for the defence, and I used similar methods to what I had used in Kiseljak, that means visiting of certain front lines, define the front line, the reserve front line and others. For the most part, we worked on building fortifications in terms of engineering work. A special problem in Central Bosnia was the climate, that is, the coming of winter. This is mountainous terrain with very severe winters, and we had to pay special attention to provisions and supplies for these municipal staffs. The road to Jajce was passable only in summer and early fall, these were mountain roads, and the rest of the roads are already under the control of the Serbian forces. Apart from these priorities, I also tried, as much as I could, to establish the command itself, that is, the regional staff command, because apart from the deputy and this one assistant and the two secretaries, there was literally no one there. There were problems in terms of the pool of people from whom I could select. There were also problems in the lack of standardised organisational documents, in other words, documents that would be used to fill the staff and which defined competences within the command. At that time, we did not have the mobilisation chart nor the mobilisation code or any other organisational documents, so that we had over 20 municipal staffs and each one had different organisation. Some had five, some had a staff of fifteen, some had a staff of one. In addition to this task, I also tried to find out ways for a post-combat recuperation period for the wounded because we had some wartime hospitals like in Jajce but we did not have enough beds for all the wounded. I also tried to set up a system of assistance to the most threatened fronts, like in Jajce, Bugojno, and Teslic; in other words, to use those points which were behind the most threatened front lines so that they could help the points at the front lines so that we could gain some time before we got better organised. Also, I tried to organise the training of personnel, both soldiers and the command staff; however, for a long time, this remained just a good intention simply because we had been under attack for a long time. I also thought at that time that Vitez should have the central command post, in view of what our assessment of the future developments were, and I thought of setting up a logistics base because the regional headquarters had none at that time, neither a logistics base nor any kind of logistics. The logistics was the duty of municipal staffs, and they handled it as best they could. Fojnica, which is a municipality which was potentially very convenient even before the war broke out, was identified as being especially fitting for the setting up of a wartime hospital and rehabilitation of the wounded, and this is what we later did. I also tried to set up at least draft documents because we did not have documents which defined either the competences or the daily activities, and let me just give you an example. The gentleman who was my assistant for information was trained as an economist. He was somebody who worked pretty much -- who had a career as an economist and never worked in information, and overnight, he just became an assistant for information, and he told me himself that he did not have the vaguest idea what he was supposed to do. Also, my deputy, Mr. Luka Sekerija, was not a professional soldier at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you talked about documents which formed the basis of your activities and through one of these, Exhibit D244 (sic) speaks to this. Was this a job that would be typically -- a type of document that a person in your position would draft?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. These are very strategic documents so that the Defence department would be the institution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Give us a brief reminder of the contents of that document because now we are having the witness talk about this document, and I heard 240, that was the number I heard, and on the transcript, 244. Are you talking about the organisational chart?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Document D240 is the document relating to the establishment of brigades in Central Bosnia, and so I link that question to the question: Was it usual or normal for a commander of this rank to issue such a document? This document regulates the establishment of brigades in the entire zone of responsibility of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Has the Prosecution found it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, we have it here on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am not going to go into this document, but just to remind you that the establishment of a number of brigades was ordered through this document. Would this be part of your competence according to the military doctrine, and did you try to set up all the necessary documents or did you receive them from the main headquarters?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This document would not be part of the competence of the -- not even the main headquarters. This document should have been drafted by the Ministry of Defence on the basis of the mobilisation development; however, this document was drafted after the loss of many positions, and it was our attempt to try to do something in terms of organisation because we just could not wait any longer to receive a document from a higher authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How about the other establishment documents which, as you said, you tried to draft and which would serve as a base for establishing some type of an army? Were such documents also of that level where you should have received them from the Ministry of Defence rather than draft them yourself on the ground?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was the very same problem, and let me just give you an example. At that time, there were 22 municipal staffs in the Operative Zone and then there was the city of Sarajevo which had two or three such staffs. No municipal staff had a standard which would regulate its organisation, its structure; and as I mentioned, the assistant for information whom I mentioned, he did not know what his job description was. So in July of 1992, I sent a proposal for the structure of the municipal staffs and I tried to define their competence, and I personally worked on instructions for assistance, for information, of trying to help them and enable them to conduct or carry out their jobs. There were other organisational documents because the situation on the ground and the general situation required that we have them and we could just not wait for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we then say that these organisational documents are a prerequisite for establishment of any army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they are basic documents for establishing any kind of organisation and regulate competences. Without them, you could not make any progress in terms of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We described briefly the situation in the Operative Zone in Central Bosnia, and then you also listed the front. We are not going to go into details of which fronts were active in which period. We will go back to that once we have copies of the map. I would like to take you to an incident, to the first incident which has been mentioned in the indictment, which is the conflict in Duhri in Kiseljak municipality sometime in August of 1992. Could you describe to us, based on your best recollection, how this conflict broke out, what preceded it, how it developed, and how it was resolved?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: With the Trial Chamber's permission, I would like to use the model again, or should I just describe it first?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why don't you step towards the model and look at the individual positions of individual units, and if you could just define all the symbols on the map? I would also like to ask that the map be brought closer because at one point we will ask that a photograph, a still photograph, be taken of it which we will submit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just before we begin -- if we could take a look at it just before we begin with the testimony? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Could we have the microphone switched on, and perhaps for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, Kiseljak is now -- we have changed the model, the position of the model, and Kiseljak is now facing Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's not change the model too many times or we're not going to know what we're doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The mountains are further away from you so you have a better view of the model.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Show us again, please, Kiseljak, General Blaskic. I have to find where I am here.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Kiseljak (indicating).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. And Vitez then ...

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik, and Zepce (indicating).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Moving here. In Kiseljak, in the same building, here the commander of the Territorial Defence staff was Mr. Sead Sinanbasic, and here the commander was, for the municipal headquarters of the HVO, Mr. Ivica Rajic. These two flags represent that building and their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: For purposes of clarification, Mr. Ivica Rajic replaced you when you became commander of the regional headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This was the situation as it stood on the 6th, between the 6th and 7th of August, 1992. On the main road running from Busovaca to Kiseljak and Ilidza and further on towards Sarajevo (indicating), that's the main road, we had checkpoints set up of the reserve formation of the civilian police. There was a checkpoint at Brestovsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was that a joint Croatian-Muslim civilian police force?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And it is denoted with a blue and green flag.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Gromiljak checkpoint was here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Once again, a joint Croatian-Muslim police force.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And here, there are no markings, but this is where the checkpoint at Brnjaci was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who controlled that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The reserve force of the Croatian-Muslim police force. The front line, the main front line towards the Sarajevo and Romanija corps, the Serbian one, of the HVO was at Kokoska. Then we have feature 651, Pljesevac, Ostrik (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: For purposes of the record, they are the blue flags.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who held those posts where the blue flags are towards the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These positions were held by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: For purposes of the record, may we note that the Serb positions are denoted by red flags; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May we now have a picture taken of the front line toward the Serbs? May we have a still, a photograph, which we could use later on as an exhibit, if that is at all possible? If it is not possible now, we can do that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The positions to the right or south-east were held by a detachment of the Territorial Defence force of Kiseljak composed of TG-1. Those are the Koscan positions and the area of the Hadzici municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: They are the green flags; right? They are the green flags opposite the red Serbian flags?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 7th of August, 1992, I spent most of the day in Zepce. It lies in the direction I'm pointing to (indicating). It is not on the model. I had a meeting there with the commanders of the municipality headquarters of Zepce, Maglaj, Zavidovici, Usora, and Komusina. The topic of the meeting was the critical situation in the municipal headquarters of Komusina. They include the municipalities of Teslic and the attacks which the Serbs launched on that part of the municipality under the control of the HVO in Komusina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Kiseljak, about what time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I arrived in the afternoon. I got home, that's roughly the position (indicating), and I got a telephone call at about 5.00 p.m. It was the afternoon. I'm not quite sure as to the exact time. It was about 5.00 p.m., not before that. They telephoned and said that I should appear in the Kiseljak municipality and that the meeting had been convened of the municipal assembly of Kiseljak and that I was to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is the Croatian-Muslim authority?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is the parliament of the municipality of Kiseljak which, up until then, had never convened a meeting because the conclusion of the assembly was that a municipal crisis staff would be set up, having all the competencies of an assembly. I asked what the occasion was to hold a meeting of this kind, why it was being convened, but I was told that I would find out at the meeting itself and that it was necessary that I attend the meeting. I went to the meeting, and when I arrived in the building of the municipal assembly of Kiseljak, I asked Mr. Rajic what the topic of the meeting was, and he told me, "We're already late. We're waiting for Sead Sinanbasic to arrive, and then we're going to start the meeting, and you'll hear at the meeting what the topic is." After some 10 to 15 minutes of waiting, the meeting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If you would like to sit down, if you don't need the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You can remain standing as you like. Do you still need the model?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We shall be needing the model because the point has to do with the barricades that were set up. They are the yellow areas.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The meeting started by playing a tape of the radio broadcast and a statement made by the commander of the Territorial Defence of Kiseljak, and after this tape of the statement was played in front of the members attending the meeting, the introductory address was made by the president of the municipal assembly, Josip Boro, and he then gave the floor, after that introductory address, to Mr. Rajic. Mr. Rajic took the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was said on the tape that was played to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, the tape presented untruths about the fact that in Kiseljak -- falsehoods, that in Kiseljak, it was only the Territorial Defence forces on the front line towards the army of the Republika Srpska and that only TO forces were engaged in combat activities; whereas the HVO was not in control of the positions there, but that it was trading and engaging in black marketeering with the Serbs. There were some other details that were presented, but that was the gist of the radio broadcast that was played and which, in fact, minimised, diminished, the role played by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What happened at the meeting next? Where did the problem lie?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After that, Rajic commented on the statement, and he maintained that this statement was not one that the -- that the commander of the Territorial Defence did not wish to deny the statement. He presented the view that as of that day in the joint command, when I say "joint command," I have in mind the command of the TO and the HVO of Kiseljak, and that only he was responsible there or Sead Sinanbasic. He sat at the head of the table, and Mr. Josip Boro sat there as well. I was there. I was present there. Mr. Ejub Mujic was there, who was the president of the executive council of the Kiseljak council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: He was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, a Bosnian, and he was president of the SDA party. We also had the chief of staff of the Territorial Defence of Kiseljak, Mr. Nasid Huseinbasic. This other problem that was stressed at the meeting and which, to my mind, was far more important and a far greater problem were the barricades, the roadblocks that the TO had set up on the third day. When I say "the third day," I mean the third day of July. Probably they were set up on the 5th of July. I do not know when they were actually set up, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you mean July or August?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, August. The date is the 7th of August. It is still the 7th of August. The meeting was on the 7th of August. The problem was with the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When were these barricades set up? What was the date?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If the 7th of August was the third day of the functioning of the barricades, apart from this barricade here, it was set up later on, all the others, the yellow barricades, this one --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute. If possible, would you tell us the place where the barricade was set up and the date it was set up and by whom?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is Bilalovac, the barricade at Bilalovac (indicating). It was set up at around the 5th of August. The barricade at Duhri was also set up at about the 5th of August. The Han Ploca barricade was set up the same day, once again, about the 5th of August. The barricade at Bukovica was set up about the 5th of August. The barricade at Han Ivica was set up about the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who set up all these barricades?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All these barricades were set up by the staff of the TO of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was that in agreement with the HVO or without the knowledge of the joint command?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was not in agreement with the HVO, and, in fact, the setting up of these barricades stopped movement, made movement impossible, for the civilian population of the local community of Brnjaci and the local community of Lepenica. The Lepenica local community was a particularly critical area because if an attack were to be launched by the army of the Republika Srpska, the population here had no where to withdraw to, no where to flee. May I just add that from these positions here, the Kokoska feature in particular and the Zenica slope, Zenica slope, with the means at their disposal at that time, that the Serbs had at their disposal at the time, we're speaking about weapons, they were able to directly hit the whole local community of Lepenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the aim of setting up these barricades? Did anybody explain this or was it explained during the meeting? Were you able to conclude the reasons for this during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. At the meeting, nobody explained why these barricades were being set up. I was worried about these barricades because I was conscious of the fact that the manpower from the Kiseljak municipality, the people there who were located at these positions, that is to say, at the front line towards the Serbs, on the third day had been completely cut off from any possibility of the shifts and evacuation of any possible casualties to the Kiseljak Hospital, they were cut off, and any supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. I apologise. Can you tell us whether these barricades were manned by an armed army, and can you show us where the communication lines were, that is, how the army and population moved towards Kiseljak, what direction, and how this was cut off, this communication line was cut off?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The communication line, and this is the direction, it goes from the local community of Lepenica via Han Ploca, across the local community of Brnjaci, through Duhri towards Kiseljak. That is the communication line. The barricade at Duhri was defended with a deployment of troops belonging to the Territorial Defence from Duhri, and in the course of the conflict, we noted that there were members of the Territorial Defence units which were made up of displaced persons from the area of the Ilidza municipality, who had come from the Ilidza municipality and who had been put up in Duhri and were now deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the other barricades? Were they also manned with armed men?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. In Han Ploca, there was a whole bus load of men. There were two parts to this bus, and it was red, a vivid red, and that was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
